docs.title: Elevate Load Tester
docs.text:
Team Elevate — Anant Agrawal, Piyush Singh, Vivek Pandey

Elevate Load Tester is a web application for load-testing HTTP targets. It analyzes a URL, classifies it as an API or a website, generates edge-case request payloads (for APIs) or crawls sitemap paths (for websites), runs an asynchronous Locust-based load test against it, and lets you compare past runs side by side.

  • Backend: Flask + Locust, with an SQLite job store
  • Frontend: React + Vite
  • Deployment: Docker image deployed to a k3s cluster via GitLab CI

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• API/website classification of a target URL
  • Generated edge cases plus validated custom cases
  • Asynchronous load tests; runs above 50 users run as parallel Locust processes on the same host and are merged (merged p95 is approximate)
  • Results: failure rate, average and p95 response time, per-case table (sortable, flat or grouped by category), failures grouped by type
  • Timeline charts (users, throughput, response time per second)
  • Comparison of 2–4 runs with a per-case "Changed with load" table
  • Baseline runs with regression flags, and a downloadable Markdown report
  • A local mock login API for repeatable offline testing (optionally requiring a bearer token)
  • Problem rate (5xx, 429, connection failures) next to the failure rate
  • Stop a running test, keeping partial results
  • Retry banner when the backend connection is lost during a run
  • Request headers for authenticated APIs; values are never stored
  • A CI regression gate script (exit code 0 / 1 / 2) with a manual GitLab job
  • Repeated runs (1–5) with mean ± standard deviation across repeats
  • Target guardrails: private and cloud-metadata targets refused, an "I own this target" confirmation on every load test, CORS restricted, gunicorn as non-root
  • Expected outcomes per edge case: "handled correctly" vs accepted invalid input (validation bugs) and rejected valid input
  • SLO thresholds with a PASS / FAIL verdict (results, history, comparison, report)
  • Capacity finder: step load until the SLO breaks; max sustainable users and the breaking point
  • Command-line runner (cli.py) and a GitHub Actions pipeline with a performance gate
  • One-command demo: docker compose up --build, then http://localhost:8080

Every feature is explained in plain English, with demo steps, in Features explained. How we know the product works — the measured results, test counts and the CI gate — is in Evaluation.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Analyze — submit a target URL. The backend checks that it is well-formed and reachable, then classifies it as an API or a website (websites also get a sitemap lookup).
  2. Generate — for API targets, paste a sample JSON body; the backend generates edge-case variations of it (missing fields, wrong types, boundary values, etc.).
  3. Select — tick the edge cases you want to include and confirm the selection.
  4. Run — start the load test with your chosen user count, spawn rate, and duration. The test runs asynchronously; the UI polls the job status until it completes. Runs above 50 users run as several Locust processes in parallel on the same host; their statistics are merged into one result (the merged p95 is an approximation).
  5. Compare — tick 2 to 4 completed runs (including split runs) to compare their totals side by side and see, case by case, which edge cases changed with load. Any run can also be marked as the baseline for its target, so later runs are checked for regressions automatically.

Website targets skip steps 2–3: the sitemap paths (or the URL's own path as a fallback) are load-tested directly.

docs.text:
Method Path Description GET /health, /api/health Health check — returns {"status": "ok"} POST /api/sanity-check Validate URL format and reachability ({url}); 400 {blocked_target: true} for a refused address POST /api/analyze Sanity-check (read-only HEAD → GET → OPTIONS; a 404/405 answer = reachable, method_not_allowed) + classify a target as API/website; includes sitemap info for websites ({url, headers?}); 400 {blocked_target: true} for private/metadata targets (redirect hops are checked too) POST /api/generate-edge-cases Generate edge-case payloads from a sample JSON body ({sample_input}); every case has expect ("accept" / "reject"); the first is the sample itself POST /api/validate-custom-case Check a user-written case against the sample ({sample_input, label, payload}) POST /api/confirm-selection Confirm a subset of generated cases, plus optional custom cases ({sample_input, selected_labels, custom_cases?, expectations?}); custom cases may set expect (default "reject"); expectations overrides generated ones by label POST /api/start-load-test Start an async API load test ({url, confirmed_cases, users, spawn_rate, duration_seconds, i_own_target: true, headers?, repeat?, slo?, mode?, capacity?}) — returns job_id; with repeat > 1 it is a series id. Without i_own_target: true → 400. slo: optional thresholds {p95_ms, avg_ms, max_server_error_rate_pct, max_unexpected_outcome_rate_pct, min_rps}. 429 {busy: true, active_runs, max_active_runs} when MAX_ACTIVE_RUNS (default 1) runs are already queued or running (both start endpoints). mode: "capacity" + capacity: {start_users, step_users, step_duration_seconds, max_users, early_stop?} runs a step-load capacity search (one job, needs an SLO; 409 in SQS mode) POST /api/start-website-load-test Start an async website load test ({url, sitemap_raw?, users, spawn_rate, duration_seconds, i_own_target: true, headers?, repeat?, slo?, mode?, capacity?}) — returns job_id and paths_used GET /api/load-test-status/<id> Poll a job, split-job group or repeat series (status: queued, running, completed, failed, timeout, cancelled or interrupted) — completed runs include the Locust stats, failures and per-second history CSVs, plus failure_summary, problem_rate, header_names, case_expectations, outcome_summary (handled correctly / unexpected answers), slo and, once completed, slo_verdict (PASS / FAIL with one check per threshold); capacity runs have mode: "capacity", capacity_plan and capacity (steps, max sustainable users, breaking point, headline); a series includes runs and series_summary POST /api/cancel/<id> Stop a running job, group or series (202; 409 in SQS queue mode, which is not deployed) GET /api/jobs List past runs: {jobs, job_groups}; each row has slo and slo_verdict ("PASS" / "FAIL" / null) POST /api/compare-jobs Compare 2–4 runs ({job_ids} → {jobs, case_comparison}); the original {job_id_a, job_id_b} form still works POST /api/baseline Mark a completed run as the baseline for its target ({id}) GET /api/baseline?target_url=… Get the baseline run id for a target GET /api/regressions/<id> Compare a run with its target's baseline (or with ?baseline_id=<id>)

Limits: 1–1000 users, spawn rate 1–20/s, duration 1–300 s.

docs.title: Running locally
docs.text:
The quickest way is docker compose up --build at the repository root, then http://localhost:8080 (see code/RUNBOOK.md). To run from source:

Backend (Terminal 1):

cd code
pip install -r requirements.txt
python app.py        # serves on http://localhost:5000

Frontend (Terminal 2):

cd code/frontend
npm install
npm run dev          # serves on http://localhost:5173

For a repeatable, offline target, start the mock login API in a third terminal (cd code, then python scripts/mock_target.py) and analyze http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/login — see code/scripts/README.md.

The frontend targets http://localhost:5000 by default; set VITE_API_BASE in code/frontend/.env to point at a different backend (see code/frontend/.env.example).

Jobs run in-process as background threads. The codebase also contains an SQS queue mode (worker.py, Dockerfile.worker) for a decoupled architecture; it is not deployed — future work — see code/RUNBOOK.md for details and known limitations.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Evaluation: how we know it works
docs.text:
This page explains how we measure that Elevate Load Tester does its job, and reports the numbers from real runs. Every figure here comes from a run made while building the features (12 November 2026). None of them are estimates.

The runs used the bundled mock target (code/scripts/mock_target.py), a small login API whose behaviour we control. Because we know exactly how it should behave, we can check whether the tool reports the right things.

docs.title: 1. What a correct run looks like on the mock target
docs.text:
The mock is built with known properties:

  • Correct handling. Valid credentials (demo / demo123) give 200. Missing, null, empty or wrong-type usernames and passwords, wrong credentials and a negative expiresInMins give 400.
  • Optional field. expiresInMins is optional: missing, null or 0 is accepted.
  • Three deliberate bugs: 1. expiresInMins as text: unhandled exception, 500; 2. expiresInMins above 1,000,000: unhandled exception, 500; 3. a username longer than 256 characters: accepted with 200, a validation bug.
  • Load limits. A global rate limit of 40 requests/s (beyond it, 429), and 8 workers that each spend 50–150 ms per request (about 80 requests/s). Beyond that, requests queue and latency climbs.

A correct tool should therefore:

  • find exactly the three bugs and report nothing else as wrong;
  • report a 429 as rate limiting, not as a bug;
  • put the capacity limit near the point where the mock runs out of workers.

docs.title: 3. SLO thresholds
docs.text:
Default SLO in the app: p95 ≤ 500 ms and server errors (5xx + no answer) ≤ 1%. Three more thresholds are optional: average response time, unexpected-answer rate and minimum throughput.

Run p95 Server errors Unexpected answers Verdict Evaluation run above (SLO also had unexpected ≤ 5%) 150 ms ✓ 6.23% ✗ 3.26% ✓ FAIL Browser run, 15 users × 15 s, all cases 150 ms ✓ 9.04% ✗ — FAIL CI gate config (known bugs excluded), local 160 ms ✓ 0.0% ✓ 0.0% ✓ PASS

The failures are correct: the mock really does crash on two inputs. The SLO turns that into a clear FAIL rather than a number the reader has to judge.

  • target guardrails, redirect re-checks, ownership and CORS (test_target_guard.py);
  • expected outcomes and the mock's validation bug (test_expectations.py);
  • SLO verdicts (test_slo.py);
